messages.subject: forcing variables used in rundeb
messages.body_plain:
Dear Milke,

I am now exploring the function of NicheMapR particularly rundeb function. To run this function I need a vector of body temperautre (Tbs) as well as a vector of food density (Xs).

I wan to ask that to model the animal under actual relastic environmental condition, can I susbsitute the temperature vectors and food density vector to actual temperature and food data in order to incorporate seasonal  effects on the animal? I think the temperature data can be integrated directly since the rundeb is also forced with temperature data in degree celsius. Am I correct? But for food density, I only have chl a concentration, so I need to convert the data into Jcm^-2 before running the model right?

May I ask you if my way to use the rundeb function with such forced variables is correct or not? Thank you so much.

Regards,
Martin

messages.subject: Re: forcing variables used in rundeb
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

That's right, as noted in the help for rundeb, default values for Tbs and Xs are:

Tbs  = rep(20, ndays*div), vector of body temperatures for each time step, °C

Xs  = rep(100, ndays*div), vector of food densities, J/cm2 or J/cm3

So just replace them with vectors of real data of the appropriate length for your simulation.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Problems with Parameters
messages.body_plain:
I've finally figured out what happened here, figured I'd post it for future reference! Turns out there was a typo of a minus sign on the CT_minthresh parameter. Meaning, if CT_minthresh is supposed to = 12, it was =-12.

Adam

It seems like all of the other core parameters and a lot of the thermal ones are estimated (p_Xm isn't, but I just now noticed your comments on how to calculate that here https://groups.google.com/g/nichemapr/c/uUrbSlWPxNE/m/lvNnlGLiAAAJ).

I see that it gives you a subset of parameters but not all the parameters you need, one obvious one being E_0, the energy content of the egg. If you're starting it of as an egg but it doesn't have enough energy to complete development, then you will indeed get odd looking results. But since you told it to start at stage 3, that may not be what's going wrong. Perhaps make sure first that a species that does have parameters is working properly with your script. Then only modify one parameter at a time to see where things start to go wrong. Happy to have a look at the code if you don't get anywhere. I’ve written R code that randomly pulls from the distribution of possible values that Debber calculates for each species (so for a given species, I randomly pull a single value for the Arrhenius temperature from a normal distribution between the lower 2.5% and upper 97.5%, same for the log normal distribution for energy conductance, etc) and runs these parameters through the ectotherm model, then repeats with a different set of randomly drawn parameters from the distributions for these variables.
> > >
> > > Since these are randomly drawn parameters from these distributions, I would expect to see some results where the model doesn't work. I’m positive this is a garbage in, garbage out problem, but for the life of me I can’t figure out what the garbage is. I’ve compared the values that come out of the random draws for species that are in the AddMyPet database to the exact values in AddMyPet and they seem approximate to each other.
> > >
> > > Have you seen anything like this before/is my basic premise of using Debber in this way wrong? (I can send you my code but I figured I’d ask the broader question first in case you had experienced this issue before)
> > >
> > > Fingers crossed!
> > >
> > > Adam

messages.subject: Re: forcing variables used in rundeb
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

There's food density, X, and there's feeding rate, driven by p_Xm and the half saturation constant, K. Check through the code and the DEB book to see how these terms interact. You'll see that p_Xm is temperature corrected in the code at the start, then becomes part of the function for feeding rate p_X:
          p_X <- f * p_Xm * ((X / K) / (1 + X / K)) * V ^ (2 / 3)
All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Same result at different food levels
messages.subject_clean: Same result at different food levels
messages.body_plain:
Hi again Martin - it will depend on X and K - read about the concept of the functional response in the DEB book. There's a transition between food intake being limited by searching to being limited by processing. After you reach the latter, it doesn't matter how much more food you give the animal - it's not going to change the metabolic dynamics because it's limited by the maximum assimilation rate.

All the best,
Mike

longlat <- c(-115.31660363516464, 35.17525626578658) # Mojave National Preserve
nyear <- 5
micro <- micro_global(loc = longlat, timeinterval = 365, nyear = nyear, maxshade = 60)

p.Am      8.49e+2
F.m       5.23e+0
kap.X     7.32e-1

#if(exists("L.j")==FALSE){L.j <- L.b}

# assign missing 5-par thermal response curve parameters if necessary

crepus <- 0       # crepuscular activity

minshades <- rep(0, nyear * 365)   # min available shade?
maxshades <- micro$MAXSHADES # max available shade?
# egg
# V_init <- 3e-9
# E_init <- E.0 / V_init
# E_H_init <- 0
# stage <- 0

# hatchling
# V_init <- L.b^3
# E_init <- E.m
# E_H_init <- E.Hb
# stage <- 1

# mature
# V_init <- L.p^3
# E_init <- E.m
# E_H_init <- E.Hp+2
stage <- 3

# reproduction parameters
viviparous <- 0 # live bearing (1) or egg laying (0)
clutchsize <- 5 # how many eggs per clutch?
photostart <- 1 # winter solstice is the start of the reproduction cycle
photofinish <- 2 # autumnal equinox is the end of the reproduction cycle

                del_M = 0.153, kap_X = kap.X,k_J = k.J/24,
                DEB=1,

                z.mult=z.mult,

                CT_kill = 1,
